title: Functions as values: your first delegates
tasks: select(items, where) and apply_to(items, action): take a function as an argument
by_kind(kind): return a function (a predicate) instead of a value
lights_off, lock_up, everything_off, goodnight: routines built from the pieces above
ROUTINES table, run_routine(name) and routine_names(): replace an if/elif ladder with a dictionary of functions
explanation: select() and apply_to() know nothing about devices: the behaviour arrives as an argument, which is exactly what a delegate is in other languages. by_kind() returns a function, and goodnight() is a routine that calls other routines. ROUTINES is a dispatch table, so run_routine() has no branches and the scene can build a button for every key.

hints.title: Taking functions
hints.content: select is [item for item in items if where(item)]. apply_to loops over items, calls action(item) and counts. Remember to call the function you were handed: where(item), not where.

hints.title: Returning a function
hints.content: Define an inner function inside by_kind: def matches(device): return device.spec.kind is kind, and return matches without parentheses. lights_off can then be apply_to(select(devs.values(), by_kind(Kind.LIGHT)), lambda light: light.execute("off")).

hints.title: The table
hints.content: ROUTINES = {"lights_off": lights_off, ...} stores the functions without calling them. run_routine: routine = ROUTINES.get(name); if routine is None, return an error dict; otherwise call routine(devices) and return {"ok": True, "routine": name}.

options: turn_off() runs immediately and its return value (None) is passed instead of the function
apply_to receives a copy of turn_off

checks.explanation: Parentheses mean *call it now*. To hand over the function itself, leave them off: `apply_to(lights, turn_off)`.

checks.prompt: Which Python type hint matches a C# `Func<Device, bool>` (or a Java `Predicate<Device>`)?
checks.explanation: `Callable[[arguments], return_type]`: one argument of type `Device`, returning `bool`. An `Action<Device>` has no return value, so it maps to `Callable[[Device], None]`.

checks.prompt: Why is `ROUTINES.get(name)` followed by a `None` check friendlier than `ROUTINES[name]` in `run_routine`?

options: An unknown name produces a clear message from us instead of a raw KeyError
It lets the routine run twice
Dictionaries cannot be indexed with strings

checks.explanation: The scene may send any name. With `.get` you decide what an unknown name looks like (`{'ok': False, 'error': ...}`) instead of leaking a `KeyError` across the boundary.
